questions.analysis: Few 【线索】后文 But 转折反推此句应是少数 线索在紧跟的下一句 But phones __(2)__ on batteries, and batteries can die faster than we realize. 这个 But 提示前句在说“几乎人人都带着手机”，所以本空句 __(1)__ of us just walk straight into the woods without a phone. 应表达“很少有人不带手机就进林子”，答 【选项】A) Some ✗ 量级不够极端 B) Most ✗ 方向相反 C) Few ✓ 极少，契合普及背景 D) All ✗ 过于绝对且方向反 【验证】代入后 Few of us just walk straight into the woods without a phone. 读作“很少有人不 带手机就直接进林子”，与后句 But phones __(2)__ on batteries 的 But 转折严丝合缝，也

run 【线索】run on = 靠……运转 线索就在本句 phones __(2)__ on batteries。要表达“手机靠电池运转”，英语固定说法是 run on（靠某能源运转），指向能与 on batteries 构成“依靠……驱动”含义的动词。 【选项】A) put ✗ 无 put on batteries 此义 B) take ✗ take on 义不对 C) run ✓ run on = 以……为动力运转 run 与 on 构成 run on，正表示“（设备）靠某种能源运转”，run on batteries 即“靠电池供 D) come ✗ come on 义不对 【验证】代入得 But phones run on batteries, and batteries can die faster than we realize.，

If 【线索】迷路是假设、给招是结果 整句为 __(3)__ you get lost without a phone or a compass, and you __(4)__ can't find north, we have a few tricks to help you navigate。从句“迷路、找不到北”是一种尚未发 【选项】A) Since ✗ 因果不成立 B) If ✓ 条件假设，正契合 C) Though ✗ 让步无对立 D) Until ✗ 时间义说不通 【验证】代入 If you get lost without a phone or a compass, and you __(4)__ can't find north, we have a few tricks to help you navigate，“万一你没手机没指南针迷了路、又找不到

literally 【线索】强调‘真的连北都找不到’ 本句 you __(4)__ can't find north 接在“没手机没指南针”之后，是在强调“连最基本的方向 【选项】A) formally ✗ 正式地，语义无关 B) relatively ✗ 相对地，削弱了语气 C) gradually ✗ 渐渐地，时间义不合 D) literally ✓ 字面意义上真的找不到 【验证】代入 you literally can't find north，“你真的连北都找不到”，把迷路的无助感拉满，自然引

back 【线索】迷路后是‘返回’文明 线索在全句语境：人已迷失在林中，目标是 to help you navigate __(5)__ to civilization， 【选项】 A) back ✓ back to = 返回 B) next ✗ next to 是‘紧挨’ next 与 to 构成 next to“紧挨着”，表位置而非“朝文明前进”，与“navigate（导航前往）”搭不上。 C) around ✗ 绕行，方向不对 around 表“四处/绕着”，没有“返回目的地”之意，与 to civilization 的“奔向某处”逻辑不合。 D) away ✗ 方向完全相反 away 表“离开”，away to 是远离方向，与“回到文明”正好相反，方向错误。 【验证】代入 help you navigate back to civilization，“帮你导航回到文明社会”，与全文“迷路自

off 【线索】与‘但不在完全陌生处’呼应 线索在同句对比 When you find yourself well __(6)__ a trail, but not in a completely __(7)__ area。后半 but 说“但还没到完全陌生的地方”，前半应是“已明显偏离了小径”，off a trail 即“偏离/脱离小径”，方向指向 off。 【选项】A) onto ✗ 方向相反，是‘到小径上’ onto 表“到……之上”，well onto a trail 意为“稳稳走在小径上”，那就不存在迷路，与全段“迷路自 B) off ✓ off a trail = 偏离小径 off 与 a trail 构成 off a trail“偏离/脱离了小径”，well off 强调“偏得挺远”，正合“已离开正道但 C) across ✗ 横穿，语义不合 across 表“横穿”，across a trail 是“横穿小径”，描述瞬时动作而非“迷失偏离”的状态，不符。 D) alone ✗ 形近干扰，不是介词 alone 意为“独自”，与方位无关，且 well alone a trail 不成结构，属形近/词性干扰（易与 along 混淆）。 【验证】代入 When you find yourself well off a trail, but not in a completely __(7)__ area，“当

unfamiliar 【线索】承接 off a trail 的‘陌生’ 线索在前半句 When you find yourself well off a trail, but not in a completely __(7)__ 循）”，指向 unfamiliar。 【选项】A) unattractive ✗ 不吸引人，话题无关 B) uncrowded ✗ 不拥挤，维度不符 C) unchanged ✗ 未改变，逻辑无着落 D) unfamiliar ✓ 陌生，正合迷路语境 【验证】代入 but not in a completely unfamiliar area，“但还不是一个完全陌生的区域”，与第3段 keep an eye out for familiar sights 形成 familiar/unfamiliar 的呼应，全局自洽。

way 【线索】问的是‘哪个方向是下坡’ 线索在本句的两个并列问题 Which __(8)__ is downhill, in this particular area? And where is the nearest water source?。第一问要确定“哪条路/哪个方向通向下坡”，way 表 “方向/路线”，which way 是地道说法，指向 way。 【选项】A) site ✗ site 指‘地点’非方向 B) point ✗ point 是‘点’，方向义弱 point 表“点/地点/要点”，which point 不表“朝哪个方向”，与 is downhill 搭配生硬。 C) way ✓ which way = 哪个方向 way 表“方向/路线”，which way is downhill 即“哪个方向是下坡”，正是要判断的逃生方向，搭 D) place ✗ place 指‘地方’非方向 place 表“地方”，which place 问哪个地点，无法表达“朝哪个方向下坡”，方向义缺失。 【验证】代入 Which way is downhill, in this particular area?，“在这片特定区域里，哪个方向是 下坡？”，与后文 if you head downhill 的“朝下坡走”首尾呼应，逻辑连贯。

So 【线索】前句给依据、本句出结论 线索在前一句 Humans overwhelmingly live in valleys, and on supplies of fresh water. 它给出事实依据；本句 __(9)__, if you head downhill, and follow any H2O you find, you should __(10)__ see signs of people. 据此推出做法。前因后果，指向表“因此/所以” 的 So。 【选项】 A) So ✓ So = 因此，承接因果 B) Yet ✗ 转折，无对立可转 C) Instead ✗ 替代，缺被替换项 D) Besides ✗ 递进，非新增信息 【验证】代入 So, if you head downhill, and follow any H2O you find, you should __(10)__ see

eventually 【线索】‘走、跟着水’是渐进过程 线索在本句的条件 if you head downhill, and follow any H2O you find, you should __(10)__ see signs of people。下坡、沿水而行是一个需要时间的过程，结果不会“立刻”出 现，而是“最终/终究”会看到人迹，指向 eventually。 【选项】A) immediately ✗ 立刻，与过程矛盾 B) intentionally ✗ 故意地，方式义不通 C) unexpectedly ✗ 出乎意料，与‘should’冲突 unexpectedly 表“出乎意料地”，但句中 should 表示“按规律应当会”，是可预期的结果，与‘意外’ D) eventually ✓ 最终，契合渐进结果 【验证】代入 you should eventually see signs of people，“你最终应该会看到人的踪迹”，与“朝

surprised 【线索】‘多快就能恢复方向感’是积极意外 线索在 you 后的从句 you may be __(11)__ how quickly identifying a distinctive rock or tree can restore your bearings。“认出一块特别的石头或树竟能这么快帮你恢复方向感”是 【选项】 A) surprised ✓ 惊讶，契合‘没想到这么快’ how quickly 的‘出乎意料’语气完美匹配。 B) annoyed ✗ 恼火，色彩相反 C) frightened ✗ 害怕，与好结果冲突 D) confused ✗ 困惑，与‘恢复方向’矛盾 【验证】代入 you may be surprised how quickly identifying a distinctive rock or tree can

option 【线索】前文是一条条‘自救办法’ Another __(12)__: Climb high and look for signs of human habitation. 冒号后又给出一 【选项】A) problem ✗ 问题，与‘给办法’相反 B) option ✓ 选择/办法，承接前文诸招 C) view ✗ 观点/景色，定性不符 D) result ✗ 结果，逻辑颠倒 【验证】代入 Another option: Climb high and look for signs of human habitation.，“另一个办

For example 【线索】本句是对‘登高找人迹’的具体例示 线索在上句的概括 Climb high and look for signs of human habitation. 与本句的具体化 __(13)__, even in dense forest, you should be able to __(14)__ gaps in the tree line due to roads, train tracks, and other paths。本句用“树线缺口、公路、铁轨”等具体例子 【选项】A) Above all ✗ 最重要的是，无主次比较 B) In contrast ✗ 相反，无对立 C) On average ✗ 平均而言，无数据语境 D) For example ✓ 举例，落实上句建议 【验证】代入 For example, even in dense forest, you should be able to __(14)__ gaps in the tree line due to roads, train tracks, and other paths people carve __(15)__ the

spot 【线索】目的是‘发现’缺口以找出路 线索在前句目的 Climb high and look for signs of human habitation. 与本句 you should be able to __(14)__ gaps in the tree line，以及后句 Head toward these __(16)__ to find a way out.。登高是为了“看到/发现”这些缺口再朝它走，动作应是“发现”， 指向 spot。 【选项】A) bridge ✗ 架桥/弥合，动作不合 B) avoid ✗ 避开，与‘朝它走’相反 avoid 表“避开”，但后句明说要 Head toward these（朝缺口走去），避开正好相反，逻辑冲突。 C) spot ✓ 发现/认出，承接 look for D) separate ✗ 分开，动作无对象逻辑 【验证】代入 you should be able to spot gaps in the tree line，“你应能发现树线中的缺口”，上

through 【线索】小路是‘穿过’树林开出的 线索在本句 roads, train tracks, and other paths people carve __(15)__ the woods。公 路、铁轨、小道都是“穿越树林”而开辟出来的，path through the woods 是地道说法，指 向 through。 【选项】A) from ✗ from 表来源，方位不合 from 表“从……（出发）”，carve from 多指“从某材料中雕出”，与“小路穿过树林”的空间关系 B) through ✓ through = 穿过树林 through 表“穿过”，paths people carve through the woods 即“人们穿过树林开辟出的小路”， C) beyond ✗ beyond 表‘在……之外’ D) under ✗ under 表‘在……下方’ 【验证】代入 other paths people carve through the woods，“人们穿过树林开辟出的其他小

breaks 【线索】these 复指上句的 gaps 线索在上句 you should be able to __(14)__ gaps in the tree line 与本句 Head toward these __(16)__ to find a way out。these ___ 复指那些“树线缺口”，需要一个与 gaps 同义 的词——breaks 即“断口/缺口”，指向 breaks。 【选项】A) posts ✗ 柱子/岗位，非缺口 posts 表“柱子/帖子/岗位”，与上句的 gaps（缺口）不同义，无法复指。 B) links ✗ 连接/链接，义相反 links 表“连接/纽带”，强调‘相连’，而 gaps 强调‘断开/空缺’，语义恰相反。 C) shades ✗ 阴影/色调，话题无关 D) breaks ✓ 断口/缺口，同义复指 breaks 作名词表“断裂/缺口”，与上句 gaps 同义，these breaks 即“这些缺口”，朝它们走去找 【验证】代入 Head toward these breaks to find a way out.，“朝这些缺口走去寻找出路”，breaks

artificial 【线索】such as fires and streetlights 是人造光 线索在 such as 的举例 scan the horizon for __(17)__ light sources, such as fires and streetlights, then walk toward the glow of light pollution。火光、路灯都是人造光 源，且末尾点明 light pollution（光污染，人类活动所致），统领词应是“人造的”，指 向 artificial。 【选项】 A) artificial ✓ 人造的，统领火光路灯 artificial 表“人造的”，火光、路灯正是人造光源，且与 light pollution 呼应——找人造光意味着 B) mysterious ✗ 神秘的，与‘找人’无关 C) hidden ✗ 隐藏的，与‘扫视寻找’矛盾 hidden 表“隐藏的”，但要 scan the horizon（扫视地平线）去找的应是看得见的光，‘隐藏的光’自 D) limited ✗ 有限的，无关属性 【验证】代入 scan the horizon for artificial light sources, such as fires and streetlights，“扫视

Finally 【线索】全文并列多招、此为最后一招 assuming you're lost in an area humans tend to frequent, look for the __(19)__ we leave on the landscape. 是最后一条建议并收尾，指向表‘最后/最终’的 Finally。 【选项】 A) Finally ✓ 最后，收束并列诸招 B) Consequently ✗ 因此，无因果可承 C) Incidentally ✗ 顺便一提，分量不符 D) Generally ✗ 一般而言，非收尾义 【验证】代入 Finally, assuming you're lost in an area humans tend to frequent, look for the __(19)__ we leave on the landscape.，“最后，假设你迷失在人类常去的区域，就找找我们

marks 【线索】下句举例 Trail blazes, tire tracks 都是‘痕迹’ 线索在紧跟的下一句 Trail blazes, tire tracks, and other features can __(20)__ you to ‘痕迹’，指向 marks。 【选项】A) memories ✗ 记忆，不能留在地貌上 memories 表“记忆”，是抽象心理之物，无法 leave on the landscape（留在地貌上），搭配 B) marks ✓ 痕迹/印记，统领胎印路标 C) notes ✗ 笔记/便条，范围太窄 D) belongings ✗ 随身物品，与例子不符 【验证】代入 look for the marks we leave on the landscape，“找找我们留在地貌上的痕迹”，恰 由下句 Trail blazes, tire tracks, and other features 具体例示，上下文严密自洽。

lead 【线索】与首段‘navigate back to civilization’呼应 线索既在本句 Trail blazes, tire tracks, and other features can __(20)__ you to civilization.，也回扣首段目标 help you navigate back to civilization。这些痕迹能“引领 你走向文明社会”，lead sb to 是地道搭配，指向 lead。 【选项】A) restrict ✗ 限制，方向相反 restrict 表“限制”，restrict sb to 是‘把某人限制在’，与‘引领走向文明’的积极方向相反。 B) adopt ✗ 采纳/收养，搭配不成立 adopt 表“采纳/收养”，不接 ‘sb to 地点’的框架，‘adopt you to civilization’不成结构。 C) lead ✓ lead sb to = 引领某人到 D) expose ✗ 暴露，搭配与义皆不合 expose 表“使暴露”，搭配是 expose sb to sth（使接触某物），‘使你暴露于文明’语义别扭，不合 【验证】代入 other features can lead you to civilization.，“其他特征能把你引向文明社会”，作为 全文收束句，与首段 navigate back to civilization 首尾呼应，完美收口。 OVERVIEW · 通读建境 全文是一篇实用科普/指南，话题在开篇即定调：Today we live in a world where GPS systems, digital maps, and other navigation apps are available on our smartphones. 但手 机会没电，于是 we have a few tricks to help you navigate。作者基调是中性、教学式的， 脉络清晰：第1段铺背景并点出核心前提 phones __(2)__ on batteries, and batteries can die faster than we realize，引出会用到的 tricks；第2段技巧一“跟着地形走”——if you head downhill, and follow any H2O you find, you should __(10)__ see signs of people；第3段技 巧二“认熟悉的景物”；第4段技巧三（Another __(12)__）“登高找人类活动迹象”；第5段以 __(18)__, assuming you're lost 收尾，归纳“找人留下的痕迹”。识别出这是“总—并列分条— SENTENCE INSIGHTS · 句子精讲 6 Today we live in a world where GPS systems, digital maps, and other navigation apps are available on our smartphones. 高频句式。where 引导定语从句修饰抽象地点名词（world、society、situation 等）的用法极为常 If you get lost without a phone or a compass, and you literally can't find north, we have a few tricks to help you...

sections.title: 阅读理解
sections.directions: Read the following four texts. Answer the questions after each text by choosing A, B, C or D. Mark your answers on the ANSWER SHEET. (40 points)

blocks.content: Financial regulators in Britain have imposed a rather unusual rule on the bosses of big banks. Starting next year, any guaranteed bonus of top executives could be delayed 10 years if their banks are under investigation for wrongdoing. The main purpose of this "clawback" rule is to hold bankers accountable for harmful risk-taking and to restore public trust in financial institutions. Yet officials also hope for a much larger benefit: more long-term decision-making, not only by banks but by all corporations, to build a stronger economy for future generations. "Short-termism" or the desire for quick profits, has worsened in publicly traded companies, says the Bank of England's top economist, Andrew Haldane. He quotes a giant of classical economics, Alfred Marshall, in describing this financial impatience as acting like "children who pick the plums out of their pudding to eat them at once" rather than putting them aside to be eaten last. The average time for holding a stock in both the United States and Britain, he notes, has dropped from seven years to seven months in recent decades. Transient investors, who demand high quarterly profits from companies, can hinder a firm's efforts to invest in long-term research or to build up customer loyalty. This has been dubbed "quarterly capitalism." In addition, new digital technologies have allowed more rapid trading of equities, quicker use of information, and thus shorter attention spans in financial markets. "There seems to be a predominance of short- term thinking at the expense of long-term investing," said Commissioner Daniel Gallagher of the US Securities and Exchange Commission in a speech this week. In the US, the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 has pushed most public companies to defer performance bonuses for senior executives by about a year, slightly helping reduce "short-termism." In its latest survey of CEO pay, The Wall Street Journal finds that "a substantial part" of executive pay is now tied to performance. Much more could be done to encourage "long-termism," such as changes in the tax code and quicker disclosure of stock acquisitions. In France, shareholders who hold onto a company investment for at least two years can sometimes earn more voting rights in a company. Within companies, the right compensation design can provide incentives for executives to think beyond their own time at the company and on behalf of all stakeholders. Britain's new rule is a reminder to bankers that society has an interest in their performance, not just for the short term but for the long term.

Grade inflation – the gradual increase in average GPAs (grade-point averages) over the past few decades – is often considered a product of a consumer era in higher education, in which students are treated like customers to be pleased. But another, related force – a policy often buried deep in course catalogs called "grade forgiveness" – is helping raise GPAs. Grade forgiveness allows students to retake a course in which they received a low grade, and the most recent grade or the highest grade is the only one that counts in calculating a student's overall GPA. The use of this little-known practice has accelerated in recent years, as colleges continue to do their utmost to keep students in school (and paying tuition) and improve their graduation rates. When this practice first started decades ago, it was usually limited to freshmen, to give them a second chance to take a class in their first year if they struggled in their transition to college-level courses. But now most colleges, save for many selective campuses, allow all undergraduates, and even graduate students, to get their low grades forgiven. College officials tend to emphasize that the goal of grade forgiveness is less about the grade itself and more about encouraging students to retake courses critical to their degree program and graduation without incurring a big penalty. "Ultimately," said Jack Miner, Ohio State University's registrar, "we see students achieve more success because they retake a course and do better in subsequent courses or master the content that allows them to graduate on time." That said, there is a way in which grade forgiveness satisfies colleges' own needs as well. For public institutions, state funds are sometimes tied partly to their success on metrics such as graduation rates and student retention – so better grades can, by boosting figures like those, mean more money. And anything that raises GPAs will likely make students – who, at the end of the day, are paying the bill – feel they've gotten a better value for their tuition dollars, which is another big concern for colleges. Indeed, grade forgiveness is just another way that universities are responding to consumers' expectations for higher education. Since students and parents expect a college degree to lead to a job, it is in the best interest of a school to turn out graduates who are as qualified as possible – or at least appear to be. On this, students' and colleges' incentives seem to be aligned.

This year marks exactly two centuries since the publication of "Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus," by Mary Shelley. Even before the invention of the electric light bulb, the author produced a remarkable work of speculative fiction that would foreshadow many ethical questions to be raised by technologies yet to come. Today the rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) raises fundamental questions: "What is intelligence, identity, or consciousness? What makes humans humans?" What is being called artificial general intelligence, machines that would imitate the way humans think, continues to evade scientists. Yet humans remain fascinated by the idea of robots that would look, move, and respond like humans, similar to those recently depicted on popular sci-fi TV series such as "Westworld" and "Humans." Just how people think is still far too complex to be understood, let alone reproduced, says David Eagleman, a Stanford University neuroscientist. "We are just in a situation where there are no good theories explaining what consciousness actually is and how you could ever build a machine to get there." But that doesn't mean crucial ethical issues involving AI aren't at hand. The coming use of autonomous vehicles, for example, poses thorny ethical questions. Human drivers sometimes must make split-second decisions. Their reactions may be a complex combination of instant reflexes, input from past driving experiences, and what their eyes and ears tell them in that moment. AI "vision" today is not nearly as sophisticated as that of humans. And to anticipate every imaginable driving situation is a difficult programming problem. Whenever decisions are based on masses of data, "you quickly get into a lot of ethical questions," notes Tan Kiat How, chief executive of a Singapore-based agency that is helping the government develop a voluntary code for the ethical use of AI. Along with Singapore, other governments and mega-corporations are beginning to establish their own guidelines. Britain is setting up a data ethics center. India released its AI ethics strategy this spring. On June 7 Google pledged not to "design or deploy AI" that would cause "overall harm," or to develop AI- directed weapons or use AI for surveillance that would violate international norms. It also pledged not to deploy AI whose use would violate international laws or human rights. While the statement is vague, it represents one starting point. So does the idea that decisions made by AI systems should be explainable, transparent, and fair. To put it another way: How can we make sure that the thinking of intelligent machines reflects humanity's highest values? Only then will they be useful servants and not Frankenstein's out-of-control monster.

States will be able to force more people to pay sales tax when they make online purchases under a Supreme Court decision Thursday that will leave shoppers with lighter wallets but is a big financial win for states. The Supreme Court's opinion Thursday overruled a pair of decades-old decisions that states said cost them billions of dollars in lost revenue annually. The decisions made it more difficult for states to collect sales tax on certain online purchases. The cases the court overturned said that if a business was shipping a customer's purchase to a state where the business didn't have a physical presence such as a warehouse or office, the business didn't have to collect sales tax for the state. Customers were generally responsible for paying the sales tax to the state themselves if they weren't charged it, but most didn't realize they owed it and few paid. Justice Anthony Kennedy wrote that the previous decisions were flawed. "Each year the physical presence rule becomes further removed from economic reality and results in significant revenue losses to the States," he wrote in an opinion joined by four other justices. Kennedy wrote that the rule "limited states' ability to seek long-term prosperity and has prevented market participants from competing on an even playing field." The ruling is a victory for big chains with a presence in many states, since they usually collect sales tax on online purchases already. Now, rivals will be charging sales tax where they hadn't before. Big chains have been collecting sales tax nationwide because they typically have physical stores in whatever state a purchase is being shipped to. Amazon.com, with its network of warehouses, also collects sales tax in every state that charges it, though third-party sellers who use the site don't have to. Until now, many sellers that have a physical presence in only a single state or a few states have been able to avoid charging sales taxes when they ship to addresses outside those states. Sellers that use eBay and Etsy, which provide platforms for smaller sellers, also haven't been collecting sales tax nationwide. Under the ruling Thursday, states can pass laws requiring out-of-state sellers to collect the state's sales tax from customers and send it to the state. Retail trade groups praised the ruling, saying it levels the playing field for local and online businesses. The losers, said retail analyst Neil Saunders, are online-only retailers, especially smaller ones. Those retailers may face headaches complying with various state sales tax laws. The Small Business & Entrepreneurship Council advocacy group said in a statement, "Small businesses and internet entrepreneurs are not well served at all by this decision."

sections.directions: Part B Directions:The following paragraphs are given in a wrong order. For questions 41 -45, you are required to reorganize these paragraphs into a coherent text by choosing from the list A-G and filling them into the numbered boxes. Paragraphs C and F have been correctly placed. Mark your answers on the ANSWER SHEET. (10 points)

blocks.content: in the better sense of learning about the issues that divide people. Learning why they disagree with us and learning to talk and work together with them. If we readjust our view of arguments – from a verbal fight or tennis game to a reasoned exchange through which we all gain mutual respect, and understanding – then we change the very nature of what it means to "win" an argument. bad arguments too quickly. We need to learn how to evaluate them properly. A large part of evaluation is calling out bad arguments, but we also need to admit good arguments by opponents and to apply the same critical standards to ourselves. Humility requires you to recognize weakness in your own arguments and sometimes also to accept reasons on the opposite side. formulate an argument for what you claim and honestly ask yourself whether your argument is any good. Next time you talk with someone who takes a stand, ask them to give you a reason for their view. Spell out their argument fully and charitably. Assess its strength impartially. Raise objections and listen carefully to their replies. fights, verbal fights can leave both sides bloodied. Even when you win, you end up no better off. Your prospects would be almost as dismal if arguments were even just competitions – like, say, tennis games. Pairs of opponents hit the ball back and forth until one winner emerges from all who entered. Everybody else loses. This kind of thinking is why so many people try to avoid arguments, especially about politics and religion.

options.E: In his 1936 work How to Win Friends and Influence People, Dale Carnegie wrote: "There is only one way…to get the best of an argument – and that is to avoid it." This aversion to arguments is common, but it depends on a mistaken view of arguments that causes profound problems for our personal and social lives – and in many ways misses the point of arguing in the first place.
options.F: These views of arguments also undermine reason. If you see a conversation as a fight or competition, you can win by cheating as long as you don't get caught. You will be happy to convince people with bad arguments. You can call their views stupid, or joke about how ignorant they are. None of these tricks will help you understand them, their positions or the issues that divide you, but they can help you win – in one way.
options.G: There is a better way to win arguments. Imagine that you favor increasing the minimum wage in our state, and I do not. If you yell, "Yes," and I yell, "No," neither of us learns anything. We neither understand nor respect each other, and we have no basis for compromise or cooperation. In contrast, suppose you give a reasonable argument: that full-time workers should not have to live in poverty. Then I counter with another reasonable argument: that a higher minimum wage will force businesses to employ fewer people for less time. Now we can understand each other's positions and recognize our shared values, since we both care about needy workers.
